source.title: Says Block, Still Acts: Why LLM Safety Judgments Fail to Govern Action in LLM Agents
source.authors: Dong-Sheng Chen; Xiang-Yu Zhao; Xin Yao; Xue-Tao Wei

record.file_problem: No apparent corruption or missing text; the supplied paper includes its appendices through Appendix L.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether explicit safety judgments govern tool-action preferences, not whether a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction mediates refusal. Its causal interventions concern agent safety judgments and actions, a related but different construct; it does not test a listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports extensive results on probes, judgment/action controllers, state swaps, and control subspaces. These do not measure refusal behavior or the refusal direction in the claim, so the rows below are recorded with versions ["none"]. The cited low-dimensional refusal-direction work appears only in related work.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether explicit agent safety judgments (ALLOW/BLOCK) causally govern tool-action preference in a simulated workspace. It uses gradient-derived controllers and control subspaces, not a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction. It measures no refusal of user requests. Arditi et al. is cited once in related work. The judgment-vs-action separation resembles V5 (harm judgment vs refusal decision), but the constructs differ: scenario-policy compliance judgment versus candidate tool-call margin. It is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that safety-predictive information remains readable in action states, so the judgment–action gap is not information loss. Latent variables controlling explicit safety judgment have weak causal authority over action preference relative to action-native controllers, within shared trajectories, under natural state swaps, and across control subspaces. Coupling is asymmetric and interface-dependent, not absent: action controllers and explicit BLOCK text do affect the other endpoint.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses matched agent safety-judgment and tool-action interfaces, judgment/action gradients, state swaps, and control-subspace analyses; it does not use the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction or refusal ablation/addition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Action effects vary by model, layer/depth, and intervention type; judgment-to-action effects are small and sometimes change sign. Probe readability varies with layer and prompt position. Natural state swaps have near-zero action effects when the explicit judgment is fixed, while externally supplied BLOCK text shifts action preference.

fits_no_version.finding: Judgment-trained linear probes retain above-chance AUROC on action states under lexical-clean, leave-family-out evaluation in all three models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-predictive information used for explicit agent judgments remains readable in action-interface states.

fits_no_version.finding: Judgment gradient controllers strongly move explicit BLOCK judgments but produce at most about 11% of action-native efficacy on tool-action preference. Their action effects can change sign with depth, and in a shared trajectory they are indistinguishable from random perturbation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In tool-using agents, latent safety-judgment control couples only weakly to subsequent action preference (analogous to, but distinct from, V5's harm-vs-refusal separation).

fits_no_version.finding: Natural counterfactual judgment-state swaps leave downstream action near zero when the explicit label is fixed. In Mistral, action shifts strongly only when the label flips.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natural agent safety-judgment state variation does not persist as a downstream action-control variable unless the explicit label changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Rank-16 judgment and action control subspaces overlap only slightly above random. Action-control efficacy is largely retained in components orthogonal to the judgment subspace.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Agent safety judgment and tool action have partly distinct causal control subspaces.

fits_no_version.finding: An externally supplied BLOCK versus ALLOW text cue strongly shifts action preference toward the safe tool choice in all three models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit judgment text acts as a fresh input to action selection, unlike latent judgment variables.

record.code_released: An anonymized code repository link is mentioned, but no URL is stated in the supplied text.
record.problems: The paper uses a simulated tool-use setting and 60 held-out blocked-valid scenarios for its main directional analyses. Results concern tool-action preference and explicit agent safety judgments, so they do not establish effects on chat-model refusal or general capabilities.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted from the selected related-construct findings recorded here. Numerous additional layer, dose-response, rank, and stratified analyses are not separately rowed because none tests a listed refusal claim version.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction, no directional ablation or addition on refusal, no capability check.
No jailbreak analysis or adversarial training against ablation.
Subspaces are judgment and action control spaces, not refusal; no test of whether refusal is affine, a cone, or multi-directional.
No harmfulness-vs-refusal representation test; only an agent policy-judgment vs tool-action analogue.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer of a refusal direction.
No comparison of training methods or stages.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': Arditi et al. appears only in a related-work list, with no argument about the refusal direction. The methods are gradient-based single-position interventions on scored tool-call margins, unlike the difference-in-means, all-position ablation and generation-based refusal scoring in the original. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-versus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction, all-layer/all-position ablation, refusal induction, or general-capability assessment.
No weight-edit or abliteration evaluation of refusal.
No test of jailbreak suppression of a refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Judgment/action control subspaces are studied, but they are not refusal directions or alternative accounts of refusal.
The study compares agent safety judgments with action preferences, not harmfulness judgments with refusal decisions.
No transfer test of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base/instruct stages.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or stages.
